title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks (Consolidated)
author: Avery Chen
body:
Summary:
This consolidated reference describes Redwood Inference's serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling model, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, operational runbooks, release highlights, and a curated list of known issues with mitigations. It is intended for on-call SREs, runtime engineers, and performance-focused ML engineers.

1) Overview
The serving runtime provides low-latency, high-throughput inference for text generation, chat, and embedding workloads across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Core goals: predictable P99 latency, efficient GPU utilization, graceful degradation, and measurability (tracing + token-level cost breakdown). This document centralizes design rationale, operational guidance, and reproducible benchmarking procedures.

2) Runtime architecture (high level)
- Components:
  - Inference Frontend (API gateway + auth): validates requests, enforces quotas, attaches routing metadata.
  - Router & Policy Engine: selects target model variant and route based on latency SLOs, cost-tier, region, and fallback policies.
  - Serving Workers (runtime): GPU-optimized process that executes model kernels, manages KV cache, batching, and streaming.
  - Orchestration & Autoscaler: maintains desired worker pool sizes, handles rebalancing for Dedicated pools.
  - Observability stack: per-request traces, token-level latency/cost metrics, and per-model dashboards.
- Data flow (request path): API -> Router (policy) -> select worker pool -> enqueue into worker's batching queue -> kernel execution -> stream back tokens -> observability emit.

Design constraints and guarantees:
- SLOs: default P99 latency target 250ms for short context (<512 tokens) interactive requests on Dedicated; hosted targets are body-of-SLA dependent.
- Strong isolation: PVOS boundaries for customer KV caches and pinned model weights for Dedicated deployments.
- Compatibility: fallback model variants must be semantically compatible (same tokenizer + similar spec).

3) Kernel selection and scheduling model
- Kernel catalog: each model variant maps to a preferred kernel profile (fp16, int8/quantized, fused-attention), with fallbacks. Kernels selected by runtime based on model arch, sequence length, and hardware generation (A100 vs H100 vs L4).
- Scheduling primitives:
  - Continuous batching: requests are appended to a worker-local queue; batches are emitted either when batch_size >= max_batch or when batch_timeout elapses.
  - Deadline-aware scheduling: each request carries a soft deadline derived from SLO; scheduler prioritizes packets close to deadline to meet P99.
  - Preemption windows: long-running background jobs (e.g., large sequence compilation/compaction) are scheduled during low-util windows and can be preempted by latency-critical batches.
- Heuristics used by scheduler (current, tunable):
  - batch_size target by model and seq-distribution (default 24 for LLM-7B on H100).
  - timeout: 6ms for interactive routes, 20ms for high-throughput embedding routes.
  - kv-cache warmup: co-locate repeat-requests to same worker for prefix reuse.

4) Profiling playbook (how we investigate performance regressions)
Steps (ordered):
1. Triage and reproduce
   - Collect request traceID(s) and associated metrics (latency breakdown, batch sizes, GPU utilization).
   - Re-run synthetic replay using profiling flags against same model variant and sequence distribution.
2. Narrow the layer
   - Enable per-kernel tracing (nvtx + runtime hooks) to identify hot kernels.
   - Capture GPU metrics: SM utilization, memory bandwidth, kernel launch times.
3. Identify root cause patterns
   - Increased tail due to small batches -> tune batch_timeout/batch_target.
   - Kernel fallback to less optimized path (e.g., falling back to generic attention) -> check kernel catalog mapping.
   - KV cache misses due to routing imbalance -> inspect router affinity and cache eviction policies.
4. Apply remediation and validate
   - Quick fixes: tweak batch settings (10-20% reduction in timeout), increase pool size for capacity, or pin model to a faster kernel variant.
   - Longer fixes: update kernel implementation, change compilation flags, or adjust autoscaler thresholds.
5. Postmortem & regression test
   - Document fix, add a targeted benchmark to the regression suite, and add alerting rules if not present.

Profiling tools and commands (examples):
- nvprof / Nsight Systems profiles for kernel-level timings.
- runtime debug hooks: RUNTIME_PROFILE=1 ./serve --model my-model --profile-output /tmp/profile.json
- Synthetic replay harness (python):
  python tools/replay.py --trace-id <trace> --concurrency 8 --profile --model my-model

5) Benchmarking suite (reproducible performance tests)
Principles:
- Benchmarks must be deterministic, parameterized, and source-controlled.
- Separate suites for latency-sensitive interactive workloads and throughput-oriented batch workloads.
Key artifacts:
- bench-configs/ (YAML) describing model, hardware, token distribution, and SLOs. Example:|
  model: redwood-7b-v2
  hardware: h100-80gb
  seq_distr: {p50: 64, p95: 256}
  concurrency: 16
  batch_target: 24
  timeout_ms: 6
- runner: a containerized harness that can run in CI or in a dedicated perf fleet.
- collection: artifacts collected into S3 prefix: s3://redwood-perf/bench/YYYY-MM-DD/<run-id>/

How to add a benchmark:
1. Create bench-config in git under eng-serving-runtime/bench-configs/.
2. Add a runner job and request perf pool quota.
3. Run with --replay and collect artifacts; verify against baseline.
4. If regression >5% P99, open a regression ticket linking artifacts.

6) Release notes (runtime releases highlights)
- v2026-03-01: initial public release of kernel-plug architecture; continuous batching v1.2; reduced P50 for small prompts by 18%.
- v2026-07-15: quantized int8 kernels for transformer attention; improved memory footprint enabling larger batches on 80GB GPUs.
- v2026-12-10: deadline-aware scheduler (v0.9) and preemption window orchestration; introduced token-level cost metrics in tracing pipeline.

When to roll a runtime patch:
- Security fixes (CVEs), kernel correctness, or regressions causing >10% QPS reduction or >20% P99 increase.
- Minor perf tweaks follow canary rollout: 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% with rollback window monitoring key metrics.

7) Known issues and mitigations (current as-of last_updated)
- Issue: H100 kernel sometimes falls back to slow attention kernel when sequence length hits irregular boundary.
  - Symptom: P99 spikes at specific request lengths.
  - Mitigation: pin model kernel to tested kernel_variant in pool config; update fallback mapping and add test to bench-suite.
- Issue: KV cache eviction thrashing for customers using many short-lived prefixes.
  - Symptom: cache miss rate > 30%, increased latency and GPU memory churn.
  - Mitigation: enable sticky routing for this customer or increase per-worker cache allocation.
- Issue: Quantized int8 path produces low-probability token hallucinations on a narrow prompt set.
  - Symptom: regressions in eval quality score for a targeted prompt set.
  - Mitigation: revert to fp16 kernel for affected model, create a quality regression alert and add a canary prompt set to rollout.

8) Runbooks (operational playbooks)
- High latency P99 spike (pager):
  1. Acknowledge and gather traceIDs and time window.
  2. Check autoscaler and pool saturation: kubectl top nodes / redis queue lengths.
  3. Look at batching distribution: low batch sizes -> adjust batch_timeout or add capacity.
  4. If kernel fallback suspected, pin to previous kernel variant and roll for affected routes.
  5. Post-incident: run profiling playbook, add bench-case.
- Conveyor: GPU OOMs causing worker crash:
  1. Identify process: check worker logs for OOM stack traces.
  2. If caused by model weight/page-in: ensure model weights properly sharded and limit max_context.
  3. Temporarily disable quantized path for impacted model.

10) Ownership and escalation
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime (primary).
- Escalation path: on-call -> runtime lead -> infra lead -> CTO for critical customer-impacting incidents.

Appendix: quick config table (text format)
| Setting | Default | Notes |
| batch_target | 24 | Tune per-model and hardware |
| batch_timeout_ms | 6 (interactive) / 20 (throughput) | Lower reduces latency at cost of efficiency |
| kv_cache_size_mb | 1024 | Per-worker default, increase for repeat prefixes |
| kernel_variant | auto | Use kernel_catalog to pin when needed |

References and links:
- Kernel catalog (internal): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-catalog
- Bench suite README: eng-serving-runtime/bench-configs/README.md

If you are reading this during an incident: follow the runbooks in section 8 and ping #runtime-oncall on Slack. For questions or to propose changes, open a PR against eng-serving-runtime/docs/ and request the reviewers listed in metadata.
